title: Practice: loss & metrics for classification
intro: The sequel to the practice assignment: build up a logistic regression model piece by piece — from decision boundary via probabilities to binary cross-entropy — and implement accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from scratch.

blocks.html: In classification the goal is to use the feature variables to create a decision boundary that separates the data points based on their categories. One example of such a classification algorithm is logistic regression.

Watch out! Logistic regression has the word "regression" in its name, but it is a classification algorithm. The name refers to the regression step under the hood (fitting the linear decision boundary), not to what the model does.
Building a classification model happens in four steps. Step 1: create a decision boundary. With logistic regression it is linear:

blocks.label: decision boundary (logit)
blocks.latex: l \;=\; b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \cdots + b_n x_n
blocks.caption: The value l is called the logit: a score based on the features, ranging from -∞ to +∞.

blocks.html: A higher score means a larger probability of the positive class, a lower score a larger probability of the negative class. Step 2: convert logits into probabilities. The logit must be translated into a value between 0 and 1 — that is what the sigmoid function does:

blocks.label: sigmoid
blocks.caption: Here e ≈ 2.718 is the base of the natural logarithm.

blocks.html: Step 3: use a threshold to classify. Usually 0.5: if the predicted probability is ≥ 0.5 the model predicts positive; if it is < 0.5, negative. The threshold is adjustable, depending on how cautious or risk-seeking you want to be. Step 4: compute the cross-entropy loss — the loss function for classification.

With two categories you use binary cross-entropy loss (BCE); with more than two classes the categorical cross-entropy loss. The values of \( y \) are the true classes (1 or 0); the values of \( \hat{y} \) are the predicted probabilities (between 0 and 1):

blocks.label: binary cross-entropy
blocks.caption: Punishes predicted probabilities far from the true class, logarithmically hard.

blocks.html: Your turn. The function receives the true classes and the predicted probabilities. The two np.clip lines prevent log(0) — leave them in! Fill in the rest and run the test cell.

blocks.html: Widely used metrics for classification are accuracy, precision, recall and the F1-score. All four build on the confusion matrix: a table crossing the predictions (positive/negative) with reality (positive/negative).

blocks.label: accuracy
blocks.caption: The share of predictions that are correct — everything combined.

blocks.label: precision
blocks.caption: Of everything I called positive: how much truly was? Important when a false alarm is expensive.

blocks.label: recall
blocks.caption: Of everything that is truly positive: how much did I find? Important when nothing may be missed.

blocks.label: F1-score
blocks.caption: The harmonic mean of precision and recall — a balance between the two.

blocks.html: Assignment: give an example of a scenario for each of these metrics in which you would use it. Think of: spam filters (precision), medical screening (recall), and situations with skewed class distributions (accuracy can mislead).

sections.title: Visualising: does the separating line fit?

blocks.html: Below: logistic regression with two feature variables (x1 horizontal, x2 vertical). The target has two classes: class 1 (positive) and class 0 (negative). The decision boundary is \( b_0 + b_1 x_1 + x_2 = 0 \) — drag b0 and b1 to rotate and shift the boundary, and try to separate the classes.

blocks.title: Dataset A — linearly separable
blocks.subtitle: The two classes lie apart: a straight line exists that separates them perfectly. Find it!

blocks.title: Dataset B — overlapping classes
blocks.subtitle: The clouds overlap: no straight line separates them perfectly. Every boundary is a trade-off between false positives and false negatives.

blocks.html:
Exercises (from the assignment):

  • What are the best loss values you can find for dataset A and B?
  • Which values of b0 and b1 go with them?
  • Why does the loss for dataset B stay high no matter how you slide? How would you improve it?

In the original notebook there is also a dataset C with quadratically separated data: a straight boundary can never separate it perfectly. The solution is the same as with SVMs: transform features (for example add \( x_1^2 \) and \( x_2^2 \)) or use a kernel — the data then becomes linearly separable in a higher dimension after all.
